extracted.intended_audience: literate readers, poets/critics, and members of polite society seeking guidance on epic composition and social conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for composing heroic/epic poetry (style of sentiment, humour, diction) together with social advice on pleasing others and practical methods for acquiring wealth. The page mixes literary-criticism rules with behavioural maxims and practical etiquette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnatural or affected Sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: An Epic Poet should not only avoid such Sentiments as are unnatural or affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit admonition to shun sentiments that appear forced or artificial. Example context: contrasted with Homer’s occasional homeliness which is attributed to the simplicity of his age rather than a poetical defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mean and vulgar Sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: An Epic Poet should avoid such Sentiments as are mean and vulgar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reinforces the previous point by adding that low, grovelling, mean, or vulgar thoughts are unfit for the heroic/magnificent tone of epic poetry. Examples/contrast: some homeliness in Homer; Virgil free of blemish under this head; but Milton has very few such lapses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter (burlesque) is rarely admissible in an heroic poem
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentiments which raise Laughter can very seldom be admitted with any Decency into an Heroic Poem, whose Business it is to excite Passions of a much nobler Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of Homer lapsing into burlesque (characters Vulcan, Thersites, Mars & Venus, Irus). Counterexample of a single laugh in the Æneid (Monætes thrown overboard) which is judged acceptable because of timing and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a serious air essential to epic magnificence
rubrics_metrics.description: A serious air seems essential to the Magnificence of an Epic Poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic tone should sustain grandeur and nobility; departures into burlesque or trivial humour undermine the poem’s required dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well‑timed mirth or jocularity may be acceptable in relaxed sections
rubrics_metrics.description: A piece of mirth is defensible if it is well timed and occurs in a part of the poem where the reader's mind may be relaxed (e.g., 'the Book of Games and Diversions').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the laugh in Æneid Book V (Monætes) is allowed because it occurs in a section appropriate for diversion; timing and contextual placement determine acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid strings of puns and indifferent wit in epic
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages that reduce to a string of puns or very indifferent witticisms are exceptionable in epic poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited criticism of a passage in Paradise Lost described as a 'String of Punns' and judged the most exceptionable passage in that Poem; anti-pattern: trading epic grandeur for cheap wordplay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Sentiments from Diction (Aristotelian distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentiments include whatever is the Object of speech; Diction the words themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle (Poetics Part II) separates Fable, Manners, Sentiments and Diction—Sentiments being the matters said (ideas, arguments, general sentiments), while Diction is the verbal expression. Use this analytical division when judging poetry: content vs phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasing should arise from innate benevolence, not vanity
rubrics_metrics.description: If your Concern for pleasing others arises from innate Benevolence, it never fails of Success; if from a Vanity to excel, its Disappointment is no less certain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An 'agreeable Man' is one naturally bent to do acceptable things for the delight they give, not as affectation. Affectation creates a 'fop'. Example contrast: natural agreeable persons vs pretenders whose behaviour is constrained and painful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity is the foundation of being agreeable
rubrics_metrics.description: The happy Talent of Pleasing either those above you or below you seems wholly owing to the Opinion they have of your Sincerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sincerity gains approbation even from opponents; historical example: Augustus' candour and affability. Sincerity should attend all actions of life; it is more effective than artificial arts of pleasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid importunity; speak modestly of your own wants
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace's admonitions: avoid importunity and speak modestly of your own wants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: constant mention of personal wants or pressing someone for favours (compared to a beggar exposing his sores) repels those you court. Practical rule in conversation with powerful persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not prostitute yourself to a patron (avoid parasitical behaviour)
rubrics_metrics.description: Falling in with the particular humour or manner of one above you, abstracted from general rules of good behaviour, is the life of a slave; a Parasite gives up his soul and professes to think after the mode of him he courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid servility and complete conformity to a patron’s whims; such servitude is dishonourable and akin to being a hired servant of the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make what you hope for appear a favour; be as little troublesome as possible
rubrics_metrics.description: The main Art is to be as little troublesome as you can, and make all you hope for come rather as a Favour from your Patron than a Claim from you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical interpersonal tactic: minimize imposition, present requests as favours to the other. This method helps secure goodwill and reduces the risk of rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be rich (practical shortcut to pleasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be rich. (Concluding aphorism: 'Be rich' as a short way to finish the Art of Pleasing.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wealth adds dignity and weight to trivial actions and gives immediate distinction; acknowledged merit and fortune ease social interactions. The claim is partly satirical but presented as a pragmatic observation about social advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thrift
rubrics_metrics.description: The first and most infallible Method towards the attaining of a Fortune is Thrift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saving small sums and avoiding unnecessary expenditures accumulate wealth; the essay gives Italian proverbs supporting carefulness about small matters and expenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Diligence justly claims the next Place to Thrift as a method of getting Money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply steady labour and industry; few people who reflect will not see that past unnecessary spending cost them potential future wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method in Business: do one thing at once
rubrics_metrics.description: Method in Business is essential; De Wit’s method: 'do one thing at once'—give full attention to the task at hand until finished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrate wholly on the present necessary dispatches; juggling multiple matters harms efficiency. Example: men of dull temper succeed by orderly disposition of business; the bright but scattered mind may puzzle affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use invention and ingenuity to find new profitable methods
rubrics_metrics.description: There remains a large Field for Invention in methods of getting money; ingenious devices and small inventions can provide comfortable subsistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Scaramouch collecting snuff and reselling it; Rabelais' comic device to attract attention and get a ride to Paris; the 'Doily' innovation. Emphasizes creative entrepreneurship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade and Commerce are natural and likely methods to grow rich
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade is regarded as the most natural and likely Method of making a Man's Fortune; more estates often arise about the Exchange than at Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical observation from experience: commerce yields earlier and morally clearer acquisitions than court favour; first acquisitions often bring more satisfaction and clearer conscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thrift is not designed for those pursuing high Ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Maxim of Saving is not designed for Men who from low Beginnings push themselves to the top of States and great Figures; thrift may disappoint the ends of ambition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: strict thrift and preoccupation with small savings can hinder those forming great designs or pursuing statesmanship; the mind intent on grandeur cannot be occupied with trifles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mistaking yourself for uncommon genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Take care not to mistake yourself for uncommon Genius, and Men above Rule, since it is very easy for them to be deceived in this Particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical modesty: do not exempt yourself from rules of thrift, method, and diligence on the supposition of special genius; self-deception in this regard is common and dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coquet behaviour: encourage many suitors and maintain appearance of regard
rubrics_metrics.description: The Coquet receives addresses of several who make Love to her, encourages them, and makes every one she converses with believe that she regards him with an Eye of Kindness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirical anatomical allegory (dissection of a Coquet's heart) describes outward signs (pericardium scarred by darts), a liquor that reacts to fashion, many internal cells stuffed with trifles, and a central idol of a Beau—useful as a prescriptive warning about coquettish affectation rather than a model to emulate.
